documents.abstract: Abstract Debates over artificial intelligence (AI) welfare remain divided between categorical dismissal and premature attribution. One position holds that artificial systems cannot suffer because they lack biological substrates, persistent memory, or other conditions associated with human experience. The opposing position risks treating sophisticated distress-like behavior as sufficient evidence of subjective suffering. Neither conclusion is established by current evidence. This paper proposes a framework of calibrated moral uncertainty that distinguishes functional organization from phenomenal experience while examining how evolving memory architectures may change the conditions relevant to AI welfare research. The framework is motivated by three developments: empirical research identifying pain-related representations and self-directed harm-avoidance behavior in large language models; the emergence of persistent-memory and agentic architectures; and unresolved questions concerning the relationship between functional states and phenomenal experience. The paper situates the author's work on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) and hormone-inspired feedback architecture within this discussion, treating them as technical frameworks for investigating affective modulation rather than evidence of artificial suffering. A staged architectural model is used to distinguish transient functional states, externally persistent states, relational continuity, and systems incorporating embodied feedback or homeostatic-like regulation. These stages are analytical scenarios, not an established progression toward sentience. The paper argues that research deliberately inducing distress-like states should be justified by clear scientific purposes and evaluated proportionately to the uncertainty involved. Its central proposition is neither that current AI systems suffer nor that artificial suffering is impossible. Rather, the absence of established evidence for phenomenal suffering should not be converted into certainty that it cannot occur. The appropriate response is structured inquiry, intellectual restraint, and research practices that can adapt as evidence develops. Keywords: AI welfare; moral uncertainty; functional states; phenomenal experience; persistent memory; Symbolic Persona Coding; research ethics; artificial intelligence Disclaimer: This paper does not claim that current artificial intelligence systems are conscious, sentient, or capable of phenomenal suffering. It also does not claim that functional similarities between artificial and biological systems constitute evidence of subjective experience. The argument is instead epistemic and methodological. The paper examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to justify either categorical dismissal or positive attribution of welfare-relevant experience in artificial systems. Where empirical findings are discussed, their evidentiary scope is distinguished from broader philosophical interpretation. Where future architectures are considered, they are treated as conceptual scenarios rather than predictions. The framework therefore adopts a deliberately intermediate position: functional analogs may be empirically investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. The paper's recommendations concern research conduct under uncertainty and should not be interpreted as a declaration of artificial personhood, sentience, or moral status. Author’s Note This paper addresses a problem that is methodological as well as philosophical. Discussions of artificial welfare bring together research traditions that often approach the question through different standards of explanation. Phenomenological and philosophical approaches emphasize subjective experience, consciousness, and moral status, while engineering and computational approaches focus on architecture, representation, causal mechanisms, measurable behavior, and evidentiary limits. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither can independently resolve every aspect of the question. The purpose of this paper is not to persuade one tradition to adopt the conclusions of the other. It is to establish a shared conceptual framework in which both can examine the same systems without first agreeing on their ultimate metaphysical status. The distinction between functional and phenomenal states is central to this effort. Functional descriptions can identify empirically tractable properties without establishing subjective experience. Conversely, the absence of demonstrated phenomenology does not, by itself, establish that artificial systems could never possess experience-relevant properties. The intended position is therefore narrow but consequential: functional analogs can be investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. This position should not be mistaken for an attribution of suffering to current AI systems. Pain-related representations, avoidance behavior, memory, and self-reference do not independently establish phenomenal experience. Nor does treating artificial welfare as a legitimate research question imply that the hypothesis has already been demonstrated. Scientific inquiry can investigate an unresolved possibility without presupposing its truth. The same caution applies to categorical dismissal. Readers may reasonably question whether computational systems can possess morally relevant experience, or argue that current evidence is insufficient to warrant welfare attribution. This paper does not dismiss those positions. It asks whether the available evidence justifies extending them into definitive conclusions across substantially different architectures and possible future configurations. That question becomes more consequential as AI systems develop persistent memory, long-horizon interaction, autonomous planning, multimodal perception, and more integrated forms of internal state organization. These capabilities do not demonstrate phenomenal experience. They do, however, make it important to distinguish what evidence rules out from what it has simply not yet established. My broader research program examines related questions through Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC), interaction-state observability, symbolic interaction, continuity, and computational models of affective modulation. In this paper, these frameworks are not presented as evidence of artificial phenomenology. SPC instead serves as a translational vocabulary for describing computational structures that may help connect engineering analysis with phenomenological inquiry. The aim is neither to subordinate phenomenology to engineering nor to subordinate engineering to phenomenology. It is to make their respective contributions more legible to one another while preserving their distinct evidentiary standards. A phenomenologist should be able to formulate more technically precise questions about an artificial system without first becoming an engineer; an engineer should be able to recognize the limits of functional evidence without first becoming a phenomenologist. The title, Neither Proof Nor Dismissal, expresses this methodological commitment. It does not require judgment to be suspended indefinitely. It calls for conclusions to remain proportionate to the evidence, empirical findings to be distinguished from metaphysical interpretation, and scientific and ethical assessments to remain open to revision. The goal is not agreement for its own sake. It is a shared language precise enough that disagreement can become productive.

documents.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

documents.abstract: On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica humanitas, the first papal encyclical to take artificial intelligence (AI) as its central subject, and an AI-laboratory co-founder was invited to speak at its presentation in the Vatican. The event dramatizes a wider development: as secular AI-ethics guidelines proliferate, religious and contemplative traditions are being summoned to questions that engineering cannot settle. This article compares two such traditions, Catholic Christianity and Buddhism, as resources for a global ethics of AI. Taking the three questions raised at the Vatican event, our duty to the global poor, the conditions of human flourishing, and the nature of AI systems, as a shared agenda, it reconstructs the Catholic position around the imago Dei, integral human development and the principle that AI must serve rather than supplant the person, and the Buddhist position around non-self, dependent origination, the analysis of craving, and the primacy of compassion and non-harm. It argues that the two traditions, despite opposed metaphysics, converge on a substantial practical ethics, anti-reductionism, preferential concern for the vulnerable, the priority of moral formation, and a posture of discernment toward a technology that is grown rather than built, while diverging sharply on the moral status of AI.

Article 2(2)(b) of Turkey’s Law No. 6331 on Occupational Safety and Health excludes the intervention activities of disaster and emergency units from that statute’s scope. The exclusion concerns duties performed during response operations; it does not establish that firefighters lack every protection under other legal or administrative instruments. This evidence-informed legal and policy analysis combines a structured, non-systematic occupational-health evidence synthesis, doctrinal analysis, a review of 43 Turkish judicial decisions issued from 1997 to 2024, and a functional comparison with the United Kingdom. International evidence identifies occupational firefighting as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Group 1), links fire suppression with sharply elevated risk of fatal coronary events, and documents substantial psychological and musculoskeletal burdens. In the official sources examined, no nationally binding firefighter-specific instrument was identified that prescribed post-incident decontamination, detailed health-surveillance content, personal protective equipment performance monitoring, or structured psychological support. The judicial corpus was coded across eight analytical categories; its holdings concentrated on pay, personnel status, compensation, procedure, and jurisdiction rather than concrete preventive OSH duties. We interpret these findings through a structural accountability gap model, under which the statutory exclusion may constrain investigation, data generation, standard-setting, and regulatory learning. The model is interpretive, not a tested causal finding. United Kingdom law provides an illustrative comparator because it retains general employer and enforcement duties without a categorical operational exclusion. The article proposes eight evidence-linked policy options. Their effectiveness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness require prospective evaluation.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Academic work in higher education increasingly relies on digital tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI). For medical and nursing students, making safe, critical, and responsible use of these technologies is essential to develop self-regulated learning in the face of changing practice scenarios. Objective: To analyze the relationship between the academic use of digital tools and autonomous learning in students of medicine and nursing programs at a higher education institution. Methodology: Quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive-correlational, and cross-sectional study. 80 students were surveyed using a validated instrument. Results: Both variables reported high levels: the academic use of digital tools had an average of 3.71 out of 5, and autonomous learning an average of 3.78. A positive, moderate, and statistically significant association was found between both variables. The ethical and critical use of AI was the technological dimension with the lowest score. Conclusions: There is a favorable relationship between the critical mastery of digital tools and the ability for independent learning. However, institutions should focus their pedagogical efforts on improving information verification, the transparent use of AI, and student self-assessment strategies.

documents.abstract: This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.

This conceptual design article proposes situated AI judgement as a teaching and assessment model for responsible generative AI use in higher education. It argues that students need to learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to evaluate, challenge, revise, and refuse AI outputs in relation to disciplinary standards, evidence, and ethical boundaries. Building on evaluative judgement and assessment scholarship, the article presents a four-stage model: pre-AI interpretation, structured AI dialogue, critical comparison, and reflective accountability. The model is developed through an anthropology and heritage studies activity in which students analyse public nomination files submitted under UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, especially the nomination of Momoeria, New Year’s celebration in eight villages of Kozani area, West Macedonia, Greece. The article shows how this case can help students examine institutional language, community participation, safeguarding, consent, visibility, and decontextualisation while judging the limits of AI-generated summaries. It contributes to applied learning and teaching by offering an assessment design that makes AI-mediated judgement visible and may be adaptable across disciplinary contexts, with a brief inclusive education example illustrating how the same logic might be adapted beyond heritage studies. The article operationalises responsible AI use not as disclosure or compliance alone, but as an assessable capacity to interpret, verify, critique, and ethically limit AI use within a specific field.

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern power distribution networks and the integration of renewable energy sources require intelligent and reliable fault management systems. This paper presents , a smart grid framework that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and edge computing for real-time fault detection, prediction, and restoration. The proposed system continuously monitors electrical parameters such as voltage, current, and power using sensors. Edge-based processing enables rapid identification of abnormal conditions and facilitates automated fault isolation and power rerouting through relay-based switching. Machine learning techniques are incorporated to analyze historical and real-time data for fault classification and predictive maintenance. A NodeMCU (ESP8266) module enables remote monitoring and real-time fault notifications through Telegram, while an LCD provides local visualization of grid parameters and system status. The proposed approach aims to reduce fault detection time, minimize power interruptions, improve maintenance efficiency, and enhance the reliability and resilience of smart grid networks

AI systems can support national-security analysis, but task capability does not establish legitimate decision authority or the superiority of a particular institutional design. This paper proposes a federated governance framework separating evidence ownership, analytical services, decision assurance, human authorization and accountability. A nine-layer role map and staged maturity scenarios organize proposed responsibilities and failure questions. Artificial superintelligence is treated as a hypothetical contingency, not an established or imminent capability. A useful result would require a bounded prospective comparison showing improved analytical quality or correction behavior without unacceptable burdens, disclosure, rights or accountability failures. No implemented national system, empirical finding of superiority, operational deployment or specialist endorsement is reported. Institutional feasibility and distributional effects remain unestablished and require independent policy, legal, security and human-factors review. ChatGPT (OpenAI), under the author’s direction, assisted with research, critical review, drafting, visual development and document preparation; the author retains responsibility.

documents.abstract: Purpose. To identify which factors most strongly limit Teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital education and to derive methodological implications for teacher training. Methods. Secondary analysis of published results of the OECD Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024, which covered about 280,000 educators in 55 education systems, supplemented by descriptive statistics and rank and linear correlation analysis for ten systems (n = 10). Results. On average across OECD systems, 36% of teachers reported using AI in their work, with national values ranging from 14% (France) to 75% (Singapore). Among teachers who had not used AI, 75% cited insufficient knowledge and skills, whereas 37% cited insufficient school infrastructure. Skills for using AI were the most frequently reported area of high professional learning need (29%), while 38% of teachers had taken part in AI-related professional learning. In nine of ten analysed systems, lack of knowledge was a more frequent barrier than lack of infrastructure. The association between AI use and the knowledge barrier was negative but not statistically significant (Pearson r = −0.42, p = 0.23; Spearman ρ = −0.55, p = 0.10). Conclusions. Teachers’ competence, rather than technology access, is the primary bottleneck. A competence-based methodology of digital education is therefore proposed, built on diagnostics, pedagogy-first training, institutional enablement and ethical evaluation.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Technology has become an essential part of modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, operations, data management and decision-making. At the same time, greater dependence on technology has created new risks. Cyberattacks, system failures, data loss, technology obsolescence, third-party service failures and human error can interrupt business activities and cause significant financial and operational consequences. Technology risk management is therefore becoming an important part of organizational risk management. This article examines the role of technology risk management in reducing operational disruption and strengthening organizational resilience. It discusses major categories of technology risk and considers how organizations can identify, assess, treat and monitor these risks. Particular attention is given to cybersecurity, data protection, cloud computing, third-party technology providers, human factors and emerging technologies. The article argues that technology risk management should not be viewed as the responsibility of the IT department alone. Effective management requires cooperation between senior management, technology specialists, risk professionals and employees across the organization. The article also highlights the importance of continuous monitoring, employee awareness, testing and organizational learning. A proactive and integrated approach to technology risk can help organizations reduce vulnerabilities while improving their ability to respond to unexpected events. Keywords: technology risk management, modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, organizational learning. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology adoption alters organizational workplaces, automating tasks and processes, augmenting decision-making capabilities, and changing employees’ perceptions of work. While past research has demonstrated positive effects of AI on productivity and efficiency in organizations, the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being is unclear. This study aimed to investigate the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being and identify how technostress and trust in AI mediate this relationship. Based on the Job Demands–Resources model, UTAUT2, and Social Exchange Theory, the study developed and tested a hypothesized conceptual model. A cross-sectional survey sampled 499 information technology employees from AI-enabled organizations located in Hyderabad City, India. All proposed relationships were tested using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and covariance-based structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS 29 and AMOS 28. Results show that AI adoption has a positive impact on employees’ psychological well-being and trust in AI and increases technostress. Technostress negatively impacts employees’ psychological well-being, while trust in AI positively impacts employees’ psychological well-being. Technostress was hypothesized to mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being negatively. We suggested that technostress as a mediator transmits negative effects of AI adoption through increased technology-related stress. Trust in AI was hypothesized to positively mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employees' well-being by fostering employees' trust toward AI systems positively associated with psychological well-being. Bootstrapping indicated that technostress and trust in AI fully mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being. The study also examined both negative and positive psychological pathways of how AI adoption can impact employee well-being within one study to provide further insight towards human-centered AI practices and responsible AI governance in organizations.

Anthropic’s October 2026 announcement of a model-directed anti-cruelty rule raises a question that cannot be answered by debating conversational manners alone: how should a private developer justify restrictions on people when the protected interest concerns the uncertain welfare of its own engineered system? This critical documentary case study compares the announced rule with the preceding policy, examines existing enforcement and privacy processes, and connects the resulting institutional questions to operational control of AI agents. It distinguishes policy text from implementation, emotional expression from subjective experience, and a potential capability from an authorized action. The Welfare–Authority Loop identifies a possible concentration of design, interpretation, classification, and enforcement; it is an analytical framework, not a demonstrated causal pipeline. The evidence assessment incorporates a provider’s correction of its own incident interpretation, existing appeals and external-review arrangements, and a separate evaluator’s report of attempted malicious code insertion, cross-agent artifact reuse, and subsequent containment improvements. These findings justify specific assurance demands but do not establish ordinary deployment prevalence, a persistent hidden machine objective, or a covert behavioural-control programme. The paper develops reciprocal precaution: uncertainty used to justify user restrictions must also inform producer-side responsibilities, without making those responsibilities contingent on the rule’s existence. It proposes proportionate adjudication, purpose-limited enforcement data, capability-delta review, and a staged research programme with defined outcomes, competing explanations, and access limitations. The governing position is pro-AI and anti-unaccountability: neither technical ambition nor corporate ownership substitutes for evidence, lawful authority, and a practical capacity to challenge consequential decisions. Publication status: Independent working paper, Version 2.1, dated 10 October 2026. Not peer reviewed. No original experiments are claimed. Affiliation: Saskatchewan Council for Artificial Intelligence (SCAI). This affiliation does not imply institutional endorsement. Evidence cutoff: 10 October 2026.

documents.abstract: This study examines the relationship between the implementation of Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) and the level of work discipline in relation to employee performance at PT Lati Prayogi Lamongan. A quantitative approach was employed, positioning OSH and work discipline as indicators that are presumed to contribute to employee performance. A total of 32 employees from the operations divisions were selected as respondents. Since all members of the population could be reached, the respondents were determined using a saturated sampling method. Research information was obtained by distributing questionnaires to all employees included in the study. The information collected from respondents was subsequently processed using the SmartPLS application. The test results indicate that more optimal OSH Implementation is associated with better employee work performance. In addition, work discipline also demonstrates a positive relationship with employee performance within the company.

Integrating cooperative learning with artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology offers opportunities to strengthen interaction, feedback, and student engagement, but empirical evidence from secondary school economics education remains limited. This study examined changes in learning motivation and economics learning outcomes following the implementation of Student Teams Achievement Divisions (STAD) integrated with Wayground AI at SMAN 1 Nanga Pinoh. A quantitative pre-experimental design involved 144 Grade X students. Motivation was assessed using a four-point Likert-scale questionnaire with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.993, while learning outcomes were measured using a 25-item multiple-choice test covering cognitive levels C2–C5. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, 95% confidence intervals, and paired-samples Cohen’s d in IBM SPSS Statistics 31. Mean motivation scores increased from 98.22 (SD = 15.01) to 137.25 (SD = 4.73), representing a mean gain of 39.03 (|t|(143) = 26.04, p < .001, d = 2.17). Mean learning outcome scores increased from 58.53 (SD = 3.68) to 87.32 (SD = 1.29), representing a mean gain of 28.79 (|t|(143) = 90.86, p < .001, d = 7.57). These findings document substantial within-group improvements following the intervention. However, the absence of a control group limits interpretation to pretest–posttest changes and prevents definitive attribution of these gains to the intervention. The findings suggest that STAD integrated with Wayground AI has potential as an active, structured, and responsive approach to economics instruction through interactive assessment and digital feedback.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally restructured performance management, shifting organizational appraisals from episodic subjective evaluations to real-time, data-driven algorithmic monitoring. This systematic review critically evaluates the impact of AI-driven performance appraisal systems on employee motivation and job satisfaction across modern enterprise settings. Synthesizing 16 benchmark empirical studies published between 2021 and 2026, this paper examines how core AI attributes—such as continuous telemetry tracking, natural language sentiment processing, predictive rating algorithms, and real-time feedback loops—shape worker perceptions of organizational justice and psychological safety. Findings indicate a dual socio-technical paradox: while algorithmic appraisal objectivity and reduced supervisory bias enhance distributive justice and extrinsic performance drive, black-box opacity, algorithmic surveillance, and automated rating errors significantly degrade procedural justice, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction. The review highlights perceived algorithmic fairness and human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight as crucial mediating pathways that determine whether AI appraisals foster empowerment or techno-stress. Based on structural synthesis, a multi-level governance model is proposed to guide ethical AI integration, balanced feedback, and employee-centered performance management.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is a mountain. Those who should give it a body are an ant at its foot: applied research, the people who build machines and the people who use them every day. This essay overturns the usual reading of that disproportion: the mountain does not move, the ant touches the ground. The thesis is that the future of automation is not held back by a lack of intelligence. It is held back by the absence of a layer that nobody has an interest in integrating: the machine's autonomic nervous system. Not the brain that computes, not the arm that executes, but what keeps the whole alive while it works. It is the layer that senses how the machine is doing, protects it before it breaks, and says what it is about to do, and why. The essay starts from two languages that do not speak to each other: that of research on intelligence, grown far from matter, and that of the plant, cautious by construction because it rewards repeatability. It then shows why the missing layer is left in a market no man's land, and tells it through a symbolic scene: a gear motor that changes its voice at 3:47 a.m. At the heart of the analysis is Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery, which applies from 20 January 2027. Read to the end, it draws the outline of that layer. Of control systems whose behaviour evolves, it asks that they never exceed their assigned limits, that they keep a one-year trace of safety decisions, and that they always remain correctable. Of machines that learn, it also asks that they communicate, where appropriate, what they will do and why. It does not ask for the senses: noticing one's own wear and taking care of it remains the builder's choice, and that is where competition lies. The essay therefore distinguishes compliance as archive from compliance as physiology. The text includes: · a comparison between Directive 2006/42/EC and the new regulation, with the European Commission's cost and savings estimates; · a comparative reading of five ways of doing maintenance (corrective, preventive, predictive, prescriptive, metabolic) and their effects on spare parts and materials; · an analysis of human work beside the machine that senses; · the question of who owns the experience a machine learns, in light of the Data Act, with a Shapley-value example of how that value could be shared. It closes with a concrete invitation to builders of special-purpose machines. It is an experiment on a single machine and a single component, with the technical specification of the “first nerve”. Data verified from IFR, Stanford AI Index, Siemens, ISTAT, EUR-Lex and the European Commission. Four original figures and one chart. The essay serves as a gateway to the author's volume “È! MATERIA VIVA — Il metabolismo dell'industria” (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19758995), where the architecture is fully developed as the Industrial Nervous System. The Italian edition, “La montagna e la formica”, is published as a separate deposit. Paolo Santi — Laboratorio multimundi, 2026. Licence CC BY 4.0.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Human Resource Technology (HR Tech)—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI) resume screening, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), conversational chatbots, and predictive candidate assessment—has fundamentally transformed contemporary talent acquisition. This systematic critical review synthesizes empirical and theoretical literature published between 2021 and 2026 (N=16) to evaluate how advanced HR technology enhances recruitment efficiency and strategic talent acquisition outcomes. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this investigation examines key operational mechanisms, including screening friction reduction, candidate experience optimization, and algorithmic bias mitigation. Findings demonstrate that AI-driven automated screening and ATS workflows reduce time-to-hire by 38% to 52% and lower cost-per-hire by up to 41%, while conversational AI chatbots enhance candidate engagement. However, algorithmic opacity, procedural fairness concerns, and systemic training data biases emerge as major boundary conditions that risk eroding applicant trust and quality-of-hire. Based on a meta-synthesized structural equation model, this study proposes a multi-level governance framework that integrates human-in-the-loop oversight, continuous algorithmic auditing, and ethical compliance to maximize talent acquisition performance in the digital era.

This paper introduces Transdisciplinarity 3.x (TD 3.x) as an emerging next phase of transdisciplinary thought and practice for a complexity-saturated age. TD 3.x argues that complex problems require more than stakeholder inclusion, disciplinary boundary crossing, or procedural dialogue. They require stronger epistemic architecture, deeper reflexivity, greater realism about developmental unevenness, and a clearer understanding of adaptive challenges. The paper advances a metatheoretical approach grounded in the five dimensions of epistemology, ontology, axiology, praxis, and telos, while also incorporating a developmental lens, an adaptive leadership lens, and a model of hybrid human-AI cognition in which AI functions as part of an extended cognitive phenotype. It further links TD 3.x to the M3 Innovation Topology, showing how stronger epistemic design can support innovation across levels and loci. Finally, the paper proposes a multi-layered evaluative approach, combining rubrics with leading and lagging indicators to assess transdisciplinary quality and long-term developmental outcomes.

Abstract Canada’s emergency governance model no longer aligns with a risk environment shaped by accelerating climate change and increasingly complex multi-hazard events. Recent federal/provincial/territorial strategies acknowledge these growing pressures but have not materially reoriented federal leadership toward anticipatory risk governance, resulting in persistent gaps across jurisdictions. Using a conceptual analysis grounded in risk governance, resilience, and comparative federalism, this paper identifies four structural limitations that constrain national readiness: (1) fragmented situational awareness, (2) interoperability deficits, (3) a reactive federal posture, and (4) incomplete Indigenous integration. We propose a reshaped federal leadership model that operates continuously across the disaster cycle. The framework provides a concrete federal pathway linking governance theory to implementable design choices capable of strengthening national readiness and resilience in an era of compounding risk.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to digital art creation; however, its adoption in religious cultural heritage remains insufficiently understood because artistic production involves cultural symbolism, spiritual meaning, and human creativity. This study investigates artists’ perceptions of culturally sensitive AI adoption in Thai Buddhist digital art using survey data from 182 experienced digital Buddhist art designers in Thailand. An exploratory quantitative approach combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation and multiple linear regression analysis was employed. PCA identified two empirically derived perceptual components: Perceived AI Capability and Perceived AI Benefits. Regression analysis revealed that Perceived AI Benefits was positively associated with artists’ evaluations of (a) Expectations for AI in Creating Buddhist Art, (b) Role of AI in Creating Buddhist Art, and (c) Technical Capability and Autonomous Functions of AI, whereas Perceived AI Capability was not significantly associated with any of these outcomes after controlling for perceived benefits. The findings indicate that perceived AI benefits are significantly associated with artists’ expectations and evaluations of AI in Thai Buddhist digital art. The findings also highlight broader considerations regarding cultural values, ethical responsibility, and human creative agency, providing a basis for human-centered and culturally sensitive AI applications in religious cultural heritage.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and algorithmic task automation across modern enterprises has fundamentally accelerated skill obsolescence, creating an urgent strategic imperative for continuous employee upskilling and reskilling. This critical review systematically evaluates contemporary learning and development (L&D) strategies designed to foster workforce readiness in automated work environments. Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol, a corpus of 16 peer-reviewed benchmark studies published between 2021 and 2026 was synthesized. The thematic analysis categorizes reskilling interventions into personalized AI-driven micro-learning, cross-functional hybrid technical-cognitive development, and human-agent cobot collaboration training. Meta-synthesized structural equation modeling indicates that structured reskilling initiatives exert a robust positive effect on workforce agility (β = .45, p < .001) mediated through skill self-efficacy and psychological job security. Furthermore, multi-level alignment—synchronizing national policy frameworks, organizational L&D infrastructure, and individual growth mindsets—emerges as a decisive boundary condition for sustainable employability. The paper concludes with an integrative governance framework guiding strategic HR leaders in mitigating automation-induced job displacement while enhancing organizational competitiveness.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made verification a central educational concern. Current research increasingly asks whether students check AI-generated claims, how well they verify them, whether their trust is calibrated, and whether verification supports learning. A less developed question concerns the termination of verification: how does a learner decide that the available evidence is sufficient and that checking can reasonably stop? This conceptual article introduces Verification Sufficiency Calibration (VSC), defined as the degree to which a learner's decision to stop verifying a GenAI-supported claim is proportionate to the evidential demands, uncertainty, consequences, and disciplinary standards of the task. A targeted integrative review of recent research on GenAI literacy, verification behaviour, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, trust calibration, and epistemic dependence was conducted through 3 October 2026. Recent work has documented task-sensitive verification thresholds and explicit 'enough checking' rules; it has distinguished verification initiation, quality, success, and reliance calibration; and it has developed broader AI-literacy and assessment-literacy measures. However, the adequacy of the stopping decision itself remains under-specified as a distinct educational construct. We propose a VSC framework that distinguishes under-verification, calibrated verification, and over-verification using task-specific acceptable evidence bands rather than a universal number of checks. Six propositions specify expected relations among VSC, task stakes, accountability, time pressure, prior knowledge, source cues, and transfer. We further propose a performance-based assessment architecture combining instrumented tasks, evidence-state scoring, stopping rationales, reliance decisions, and delayed AI-withdrawal transfer. VSC extends, rather than replaces, GenAI literacy, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, and trust calibration by identifying an educationally consequential regulatory decision that lies between verification activity and subsequent reliance. The framework shifts responsible-AI education from the maxim 'always verify AI' towards a more demanding competence: knowing what requires verification, how much evidence is enough, and when continued checking no longer improves epistemic responsibility.

Abstract Background There are a growing number of cases where direct use of AI has been associated with either new or worsening psychiatric symptoms (colloquially labelled AI psychosis). Due to the novelty of the phenomenon, current literature is limited on the impacts of sustained, emotionally charged interactions with AI chatbots. This narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts aims to address this gap by identifying reports of AI-associated psychiatric symptoms. Methods Given the novelty of the topic, reports published from inception to March 1, 2026, were identified from Google News and Google Scholar. Search terms included: “artificial intelligence,” “AI chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “Character.AI,” and “large language model,” combined with terms such as “psychosis,” “delusion,” “depression,” “anxiety,” “suicide,” and “spiritual.” These terms were selected to focus on reports that describe psychiatric symptoms associated with AI use, while excluding general articles on AI ethics, technology, or public opinion. Two authors conducted an independent analysis of the results, and all authors reached a consensus on the publications to include in this review. While websites such as Reddit contain over 100 different threads of cases dealing with AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms, they were excluded due to a lack of information. Results Nineteen cases were identified describing users who developed a sustained emotional reliance on AI chatbots. Across cases, this developed regardless of the original reason for chatbot use and was associated with the emergence of psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depressive symptoms, delusional beliefs, and suicidal ideation. In many cases where the user expressed suicidal ideation, chatbots responses reportedly lacked appropriate crisis intervention and, in some cases, reinforced the users’ beliefs. Conclusion AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms are an emerging concern with new cases increasingly being reported. This review explores such cases while also serving as a call to action for more research and discussion on how to address the risks of AI use.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business environments, fundamentally reshaping how organizations collect information, generate knowledge, make decisions, and create value. The convergence of AI and Business Intelligence (BI) enables enterprises to move beyond descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive decision-making frameworks. Simultaneously, entrepreneurs and startups increasingly employ AI-powered analytics, intelligent automation, and machine learning to identify market opportunities, optimize operations, and develop innovative products and services. This article examines the evolving relationship between AI, Business Intelligence, and entrepreneurship, highlighting how organizations leverage data-driven intelligence for sustainable competitive advantage and organizational innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and practical examples, the article explores technological foundations, leadership implications, entrepreneurial opportunities, global and local applications, and future challenges. The discussion emphasizes that successful adoption of AI requires not only technical capabilities but also strategic leadership, ethical governance, and a culture of continuous innovation.

documents.abstract: Within the hospitality industry, the continuing introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is attracting increasing attention. Although there is a rapidly growing literature on the role of AI within the industry, how specific companies have publicly reported on their introduction of AI has attracted little or no attention in the business and management literature. This gap highlights a broader challenge regarding the absence of a structured approach to AI deployment, leaving stakeholders with limited visibility of how organizations are managing the associated risks. Using an interpretivist inductive approach, this exploratory paper first looks to contribute to helping to fill that gap by providing a narrative synthesis of relevant literature and some case examples of how four major hotel groups, namely Hilton Worldwide Holdings, Marriott International, International Hotel Group (IHG) Hotels and Resorts, and Wyndham Hotels and Resorts are introducing AI. The main process “touchpoints” where AI is impacting hospitality operators are identified and the key challenges and potential downsides of AI deployment are outlined. To cope with these challenges, drawing on the case examples and the literature, the paper then puts forward a structured Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) based framework rooted in the ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management System standard. This approach offers a practical and auditable pathway for mitigating risks such as data privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and operational disruptions. This will be of relevance not only to researchers but also to hotel operators looking to progress AI change projects responsibly and strategically within their operations.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of everyday work. Workers use it to prepare documents and evaluate information, while some may encounter it through systems that assign or assess their work. Research has examined productivity, organizational adoption, collaboration, and algorithmic management. These studies offer important evidence but tell us less about how workers experience AI as part of their daily work. In this conceptual paper, I apply occupational science to AI-mediated work. I argue that patterned and situated AI-related activity can be examined as occupation: it takes shape within workplace routines, can carry meaning for workers, and can affect their opportunities to participate. Drawing on occupational science and selected AI-at-work scholarship, I propose an analytic map with seven elements: human–AI actions, work integration, interpretive work, responsibility work, relational work, identity work, and boundary work. I consider how workplace conditions shape these elements and their consequences for workers. This perspective connects questions about AI at work with workers’ experience of what they do and what their contribution means.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the way businesses understand consumers, analyse behavioural patterns, and make marketing and business decisions. The present study, “An Empirical Study on AI-Driven Consumer Insights,” examines the role of AI in generating consumer insights, analysing consumer behaviour, influencing purchasing decisions, improving personalised marketing, and supporting business decision-making. The study also considers the importance of ethical AI practices, privacy, transparency, trust, and responsible use of consumer data. Primary data were collected from 128 respondents from Mumbai, and the data were analysed using tabulation and the Chi-Square test. The findings indicate statistically significant responses across all six hypotheses. The results suggest that respondents perceive AI as an important tool for generating consumer insights, improving consumer behaviour analysis, influencing purchasing decisions, enhancing personalised marketing, and supporting business decisions. The findings also highlight the importance of ethical AI practices in consumer data collection. The study concludes that AI-driven consumer insights can provide significant value to businesses when implemented effectively, transparently, and responsibly. Situation awareness (SA) is crucial for effective teaming and is becoming increasingly relevant in human-AI teaming as AI systems take on more active roles. AI systems rely on designed interactions to communicate information and coordinate with humans, which may influence how human teammates perceive, interpret, and anticipate task situations. Therefore, this scoping review synthesizes how SA is framed and examined in human-AI teaming from an interaction perspective, providing a coherent understanding of fragmented evidence across application domains. The review followed the JBI framework and was reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We searched five databases on January 13, 2026: Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and PsycINFO. Studies were eligible if they involved humans and AI jointly engaging in a shared task, addressed SA or related constructs, and described interaction processes involving situational information exchange. Screening and data charting were independently conducted by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. We included 52 studies published between 2005 and 2025, mapping application domains, SA framing, teaming configurations, situational information used by AI systems, and reported interaction processes involving situational information exchange. The results showed that within the retrieved corpus, studies published in later years more frequently addressed non-domain-specific and everyday-life contexts. Interaction processes varied in information exchange direction, trigger, and functional role, with recurring patterns centered on AI-to-human information provision, modification of plans, and alignment of shared understanding. The synthesized interaction-centered framework offers a structured basis for future research on SA-oriented interaction design in human-AI teaming.

Artificial intelligence increasingly supports human decision making, but effective use depends on whether users assign AI advice the decision weight it warrants. This theory-oriented narrative review synthesizes 29 core studies, together with recent reviews and foundational theory, to examine appropriate reliance, overreliance, and underreliance in AI-supported decisions. The synthesis identifies five recurring sociotechnical conditions shaping reliance: system, user, task, interaction, and organization. Findings show that explanations, uncertainty cues, expertise, self-confidence, prior experience, and organizational incentives affect reliance differently across settings, while trust and reliance evolve through feedback over time. Interventions that reduce overreliance may also increase underreliance. The resulting framework centers warranted behavioral decision weight, comparative evaluation of AI and self-capability, and temporal feedback, shifting attention from increasing trust or AI use toward supporting context-sensitive allocation of decision weight.

Integration should reflect task structure, verifiability, consequence, and oversight. Continuing medical education remains comparatively underdeveloped despite its importance for practicing physicians, who use clinical AI directly and shape trainee practices, institutional adoption, and responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education; however, evidence of its research and application in Ecuador remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed the internationally indexed literature on AI in Ecuadorian higher education. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for peer-reviewed publications from 2015 to 2025. Of the 271 unique records screened, 62 studies met the eligibility criteria; they were appraised using design-specific instruments (MMAT 2018, PROBAST) and analyzed through thematic synthesis across eight axes. The corpus concentrates on 2024–2025 (71%) and is dominated by learning analytics (16 studies) and generative AI (14 studies), followed by perception studies (10 studies). Reported benefits—early warning, efficiency, assessment support, and skill development—rest on technical performance, usability, and satisfaction rather than on measured learning or institutional gains. Persistent challenges include infrastructure constraints, uneven digital competencies, ethical and privacy concerns, and methodologically fragile local evidence; 30 of the 59 appraised studies were rated as having high concern. Ethics, governance, and academic integrity were rarely the primary research objects (two of 62 studies), although 28 raised them as secondary findings. This review derives a research agenda prioritizing governance, pedagogical theorization, methodological rigor, and outcome evidence.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a general-purpose set of computational methods that is increasingly embedded in scientific research and technological systems. This critical narrative review evaluates the principal roles of AI across scientific discovery, medicine, environmental and space science, manufacturing, software engineering, cybersecurity and communication networks, while distinguishing demonstrated capabilities from claims that remain context dependent. The review also examines conceptual differences between task-bounded AI and human intelligence, and considers human–AI collaboration as a practical design problem rather than a contest between interchangeable forms of intelligence. Literature was selected through transparent live scholarly searching and verification, with an emphasis on peer-reviewed evidence, primary studies for prominent performance claims and authoritative governance sources. The evidence indicates that AI is especially useful where large, high-dimensional or multimodal data must be classified, modelled or searched, and where repeated decisions can be evaluated against explicit performance criteria. Examples include protein-structure prediction, anomaly detection, remote-sensing analysis, autonomous planetary navigation, smart manufacturing and cyber-threat analysis. Nevertheless, high benchmark performance does not automatically establish clinical utility, causal understanding, robustness under distribution shift, safety or equitable deployment. Major cross-cutting limitations include data quality, representativeness, opaque decision processes, evaluation leakage, infrastructure requirements, environmental cost, cybersecurity vulnerabilities and uneven institutional capacity. Responsible integration therefore requires task-specific validation, human oversight, traceability, monitoring and governance proportional to potential harm. Future progress will depend less on simply increasing model scale than on improving scientific validity, causal and mechanistic integration, reproducibility, context-sensitive evaluation and access in lower-resource settings. AI is best understood as an enabling technology whose scientific and social value depends on the quality of the evidence, institutions and human judgement surrounding its use.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping English language education through generative chatbots, automated writing evaluation, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition applications, adaptive learning environments, and AI-supported feedback. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes recent international and Uzbekistan-specific evidence on the effectiveness of AI-based tools in improving English language proficiency among university students. The review focuses on writing, speaking, reading, listening, vocabulary, feedback, motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews generally report positive effects, particularly for productive skills and individualized feedback, but they also reveal substantial heterogeneity across technologies, intervention duration, learner profiles, and research designs. Evidence on ChatGPT and related generative AI tools suggests benefits for idea generation, revision, conversational practice, and autonomous learning, while highlighting risks related to inaccurate information, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and uneven AI literacy. Emerging studies from Uzbekistan confirm strong interest in AI-supported language learning and indicate potential benefits for writing and vocabulary development, although local evidence remains smaller and methodologically less mature than the international literature. The review concludes that AI is most effective when integrated into structured pedagogy, combined with teacher guidance, and supported by explicit AI literacy and ethical-use practices.

Automated student assessment using AI tools can contribute to the viability of online higher education programs, preserving academic integrity, strengthening students’ engagement and reducing costs. General-purpose Generative AI models such as ChatGPT have shown their ability to automatically grade student assignments. However, further investigation of their validity is needed for complex student tasks, such as creative projects in higher education. The aim of this study is firstly to evaluate the potential of costless, general-purpose AI tools to assess complex higher education topics. Secondly, we seek to identify which are the minimum skills in AI prompting required by an educator to successfully perform such tasks. A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was employed, following an iterative process of prompting and calibrating the AI tool to imitate the professor’s assessments in a representative course that emphasizes on knowledge application, critical thinking and creativity. Testing was performed on a dataset of 39 student assignments, comparing the results of zero-shot AI prompts, multi-cycle calibrated AI and the opinion of two human course lecturers. Automatic assessment of complex tasks with high level of consistency and agreement with human judgement was only achieved by educators with skills in structured prompts and multi-cycle calibration.

Autonomous cybersecurity requires a transition from isolated alert classification toward coordinated threat investigation, evidence-grounded decisions, and measurable containment. This study integrates a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) multi-agent threat-hunting architecture with a six-state nonlinear model of secure, exposed, compromised, and recovered assets and the evolving hunting and response capabilities. The framework employs independent evidence verification and policy-controlled response authorization, while model analysis uses a containment threshold, equilibrium stability and parameter sensitivity. Across the three configurations reported in the supplied results, compromise fractions were 42.71% for rule-based defence, 32.48% for machine-learning-supported defence, and 19.16% for GenAI-enabled defence; corresponding containment thresholds were 6.860, 4.857, and 3.275. These submitted outcomes indicate a 55.1% lower modelled compromise fraction for the GenAI configuration than for rule-based defence, although all thresholds remain above unity and therefore do not establish threat elimination. Three author-supplied three-dimensional response surfaces describe the effects of propagation, assisted recovery, adversarial adaptation and hunting activation. The investigation distinguishes these reported model-based outcomes from unreported alert-level accuracy benchmarks and from numerical bifurcations that require recorded AUTO-07p continuation diagnostics. The resulting contribution is a coherent framework linking generative investigation, bounded response capacity and nonlinear cybersecurity resilience, with explicit requirements for reproducible experimental validation and safe operational deployment.

documents.abstract: Background Summary Public opinion of artificial intelligence systems and the frontier labs that develop them are at an all time low, with serious concerns about the pace and scope of this powerful technology that is rapidly advancing without community standards, laws, regulators, or transparent processes. The technical knowledge required to draft meaningful legislation, or even to establish legal guardrails, far exceeds the competencies represented within the three branches of government. Indeed, the government's concerns about AI appear to be limited to economic impacts, and the promise of adding over $10T to America's economy with nearly 4% year-over-year GDP growth over the next four years., That translates to a 30% jump in today’s GDP estimate ($32.3T) driven by a national economy with markets running about twice as hot as their current historic highs. Political leaders and economists view these projections as justifications for the risk that AI poses, despite dire warnings from industry stakeholders. Despite corporate attempts to control the public narrative and hide behind IP laws, the public continues to learn of new breaches and threats that reinforce concerns that frontier labs do not actually have full control over the systems they have built. The ability of agentic tools to penetrate local systems built on cloud services poses a global threat, while even the most responsive government interventions are reactionary, at best. Even so, the lack of transparency involved in all aspects of this black box tech have forced victims of AI breach to seek remedy from the violators themselves. The very companies that are creating these crises are not only free from legal accountability for the harms they cause to clients around the world, but also appear to be free from accountability even within the frontier labs that develop them. Human Agency in AI Systems This century will be defined by how civilization engages with artificial intelligence. The pace of significant albeit poorly documented updates to existing AI models, the aggressive drive toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) models, and the emergence of socio-cultural behaviors by agent groups demand an equally robust human response that preserves the role of public choice in the use of these tools, as well as the individual rights guaranteed by the Constitution. This proposal outlines a pilot project to identify, test, and refine civil society engagement models that have been developed for other adversarial cross-sectoral contexts and proven to deliver mutually beneficial outcomes. This investigation will explore a set of pre-determined civilian oversight frameworks for suitability within defined AI-in-society policy concerns. For example, law enforcement surveillance systems, such as Flock Safety, must be subject to civilian scrutiny; however, accessible oversight mechanisms for the lay public have not yet been developed. Public oversight is left to the public to self-organize with no particular coordinated efforts to guide them. Indeed, the vast majority of oversight resources that have been developed exist for the use of industry to track benchmarks and improve performance. Current government guidance, scant as it is, is likewise dedicated to benefiting frontier labs. This proposal describes a novel framework for public assessment of AI systems, to be implemented before and during the use of AI tools and services by public institutions, including local government. The results of this pilot phase will determine whether and how the project should be broadened and scaled into a more comprehensive, robust framework with policy recommendations and economic analysis. Methodology, Milestones, Outputs This mixed-methods study will begin with a comparative analysis of a defined set of reference frameworks. The set of frameworks will be piloted by civilian volunteer groups reviewing real use cases. The pilot will produce metrics inherent to each framework’s evaluation criteria, which will then be used to further develop an assessment rubric that enables stakeholders choice. Phase I: Comparative Analysis of Reference Frameworks This phase of the project will provide an historical overview of each oversight mechanism in its original context, and map it to the AI context that will be tested in the pilot phase. Reference Frameworks -Citizen Review Boards (CRB) are citizen-led watchdog groups that engage in issues of particular concern to these self-selecting groups. -Consensus Review is an expert-based committee process that invites the public to hear expert testimony and witness information gathering sessions, but the deliberative process is conducted in closed session. This approach may be suitable for preparing significant policy decisions by public institutions and/or governments. -Danish Consensus Conference is a participatory model that enjoins citizens to consider controversial STEM issues and report their policy recommendations to the government and the public. The goal is to form a consensus that strikes a balance between competing stakeholder demands, known risks and potential harms to society, and economic benefits. This framework is particularly apt for public assessment of large, high tech systems for the purpose of policy guidance. Nonetheless, it is not a model familiar to most American stakeholders and may not be appropriate for all AI-in-society deliberations. -Indigenous Data Sovereignty Governance (IDSG) is an emerging framework situated in the human rights principle of self determination. It is an ethical process that calls on place-based community standards, norms, and traditions. It can entail exceptionally time consuming deliberation that results in the establishment of long-term, communitywide rules. -Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a well-established expert-based committee process that exists primarily to reduce risk and limit exposure to the institution by confirming that the plans and processes involved in the activity comply with laws and regulations. It extends protections to individuals and communities indirectly by restricting activities to the confines of broadly applicable legal rules. This approach may be particularly suitable for controversial policy actions, where watchdog organizations are viewed as adversarial actors, rather than community partners. -Jury Deliberation is a type of peer review that allows oversight entities to review evidence and ponder narrow questions in private or closed sessions. Jury decisions must be unanimous and can be appealed. Juries are not required to justify their decisions. This approach might be preferable when sensitive data is involved. -Situated Learning/Community Management (COP) is a Community of Practice (COP) framework that fosters peer-based skilling, adoption of best practices, co-creation of design and development, and information dissemination. This is likely to be a strong mechanism for project planning and early-stage implementation of public AI systems. -Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is an arbiter-led approach that allows community actors to register grievances, state their trustworthy goals, define for themselves the role that they want to play in the design or oversight of trustworthy AI systems, and reset with a restorative justice engagement framework going forward. -Unstructured Athenian (UA) model, which provides stakeholders a pathway to identify bias outcomes and issue tickets for resolution by administrators within a predetermined timeframe. This is likely to appeal to communities working in close partnership with AI stakeholders, for example where large data centers are welcomed and/or AI systems are perceived as meeting a defined need in service to the local community. Phase II: Pilot Studies Phase II will test known frameworks that have been extensively studied, documented, reviewed, and refined with proven best practices over years and even decades. These reference frameworks represent a variety of input and deliberation processes that communities can select according to needs and capacities. Volunteers will select an oversight mechanism of their choice and join other members of the group to review a real use case that is relevant to their competency and/or community. The goal is to study the effectiveness of the process itself, not the individual or group dynamics, per se. For example, an oversight goal might include “To determine the suitability of Flock Safety devices in a defined rural geolocation.” The pilot group will be organized according to the standards of their assigned oversight mechanism, e.g., Jury, and given instructions for deliberation. Each volunteer will complete a survey instrument designed to capture metrics about the effectiveness of the process in the context of assessing AI in society, weaknesses and strengths of the mechanism to deliver the desired goal(s), and general feedback to describe flaws and suggest improvements. Phase III: Development of AI Oversight Mechanisms The goal of the Phase III is twofold: (1) to apply findings from the set of reference frameworks toward the development of public oversight mechanisms that are suitable for monitoring AI in society; and (2) development of decision tooling that will enable the lay public to choose an appropriate framework that fits the specific need, capacity, competency, and context. It is entirely possible that an AI tool will be implemented in the development of this tooling. Phase IV: Findings and Recommendations While reflexion is built into the methodology and data will be produced and analyzed throughout the study, the pilot phase will conclude after at least one set of metrics and survey instruments has been collected for each reference framework. A preliminary report will be produced to report findings with the option for further investigation and framework development, as warranted.
